area: Area IX. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain eights on pylons at commercial depth (the line-of-sight reference, pivotal altitude and why you climb and descend as groundspeed changes), demonstrate it from the right seat while explaining it with the bank never past 40°, and spot, explain and fix your learners' errors, above all holding the pylon with rudder.
why: Eights on pylons is the most advanced and difficult ground reference maneuver, and the AFH calls it unmatched for building intuitive control of the airplane [[24:160|AFH 7-14]]. It is flown low, in medium to steep banks, with eyes outside, and its classic mistake (yawing the wing onto the pylon with rudder) puts the airplane in uncoordinated flight near the ground [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. For ASEL the evaluator must select this Task (ACS Area IX Note), so you will fly it while teaching it.

warmup: Think first: on the first pylon turn to the left, the pylon slides back behind your learner's reference line. The learner presses left rudder, the ball swings to the right, and the pylon comes back into place. What was the airplane telling the learner, what should they have done instead, and why does this 'fix' worry you more than the original error?

key_terms.def: A prominent ground reference that the airplane turns around. Two are used, one for each half of the eight [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
The altitude at which, for a given groundspeed, the projected reference line to the pylon appears to pivot on it [[24:161|AFH 7-15]] [[24:383|AFH G-11]].
An imagined line from the pilot's eyes to the pylon, parallel to the airplane's lateral axis. It is not the wingtip [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].
Groundspeed squared, divided by 11.3 (knots) or 15 (mph), plus the MSL elevation of the pylon [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].
Speed over the ground. Lower than airspeed headed upwind, higher headed downwind [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
Heading into the wind to cancel drift; flown on the leg between the pylons [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].
The POH maneuvering airspeeds, which vary with weight; used to plan the pivotal altitudes [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
Rudder applied with aileron to cancel adverse yaw, ball centered. The horizontal component of lift turns the airplane, not the rudder [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
Uncoordinated turn in which the pilot feels pressed toward the outside of the turn [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
Uncoordinated turn in which the pilot feels pressed toward the inside of the turn [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
A stall with aileron one way and rudder the other; little warning, and it can roll toward inverted [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Absorption in one task, such as the pylon, to the exclusion of others [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

chunks.title: Eights on pylons at the CFI standard

body.p: Eights on pylons is the most advanced and difficult of the ground reference maneuvers, and the AFH calls it unmatched for developing intuitive control of the airplane [[24:160|AFH 7-14]]. In the earlier ground track maneuvers the pilot flies a set path over the ground. Here the pilot holds a lateral relationship to one spot, which trains accurate maneuvering while dividing attention between the flightpath and the pylons [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

The procedure in one breath: fly a figure eight around two pylons, turning in opposite directions, and climb or descend as groundspeed changes so the line from your eyes to the pylon stays on it [[24:160|AFH 7-14]] [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Altitude is the control that holds the pylon, bank follows from your distance to it, and the rudder only coordinates [[24:163|AFH 7-17]] [[24:164|AFH 7-18]].

rows: Establish the correct bank angle for the conditions, not to exceed 40°.
The only number in the Task. Plan entry distance so the steepest point stays at or below 40°.
Apply smooth and continuous corrections so that the line-of-sight reference line remains on the pylon.
Small, early corrections, not big ones after the pylon has moved.
Maintain pylon position using appropriate pivotal altitude, avoiding slips and skids.
Hold the pylon with altitude, with the ball centered.
Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task.
The evaluator flies errors; you name, explain and fix them.

callout.text: For ASEL the evaluator must select at least four Area IX Tasks, including Tasks E and F (ACS Area IX Note). There is no altitude tolerance in this Task because the altitude is supposed to change; the bank limit is 'not to exceed 40°' (ACS AI.IX.F.S5).

check.q: Which skill element in this Task carries a number, and what is it?

chunks.title: The line of sight, and why it is not the wingtip

body.p: The pilot imagines a line from the eyes to the pylon, parallel to the lateral axis, along which the airplane appears to pivot. Picture a taut string from the eyes to the pylon that stays parallel to the lateral axis all the way around, never at an angle to it [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

Many instructors say 'put the wingtip on the pylon.' The AFH says that interpretation is not correct: high-wing, low-wing, swept and tapered wings, and tandem or side-by-side seating all give different angles from the eye to the wingtip [[24:160|AFH 7-14]]. The line may sit ahead of, behind, above or below the wingtip, and it differs for each pilot and each seat; in side-by-side airplanes the variation is small when the pilots' eyes are at about the same level [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

bullets: On the ground, have the learner sit in the airplane and sight along the lateral axis, then note where that line crosses the wing, strut or window frame. That is their own landmark (application of [[24:160|AFH 7-14]]).
A much taller or shorter learner sees a different spot than you do; find it with each learner rather than handing over yours [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].
In a high-wing airplane the lowered wing can hide a ground point, especially in a left turn from the left seat [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. Agree on which turn shows the pylon best before you fly.
Say it the same way every time: keep the line on the pylon, not the wingtip [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

callout.text: Teach the motion in terms of the line. If the line moves ahead of the pylon, the pylon appears to move back; if the line moves behind the pylon, the pylon appears to move ahead [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Learners mix these up, so make them say which one they see before they correct.

check.q: Why does the AFH reject 'put the wingtip on the pylon'?
check.a: Different wing types and seating give different angles from the eye to the wingtip, so the true reference is a line from the eyes parallel to the lateral axis [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

chunks.title: Pivotal altitude: the rule of thumb and the reason behind it

body.p: Pivotal altitude is the altitude at which, for a given groundspeed, the projection of the reference line to the pylon appears to pivot. It is determined by groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

Rule of thumb: square the groundspeed, divide by 11.3 if it is in knots or by 15 if it is in mph, then add the MSL elevation of the pylon [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. Worked example (computed): 90 knots gives 8,100 / 11.3 = 717 feet above the pylon; with pylons at 1,050 feet MSL the altimeter target is about 1,767 feet.

Why the bank does not matter (application, not stated in the sources). The PHAK gives radius of turn = V squared / (11.26 x tangent of bank) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. Figure 7-14 draws the sight line along the lowered wing, so height above the pylon = radius x tangent of bank. Multiply them and the bank cancels: height = V squared / 11.26, close to the AFH rule. At 100 knots: 888 feet whether the radius is 1,538 feet (30°) or 888 feet (45°). The AFH itself simply states that the bank chosen does not alter the pivotal altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

bullets: Distance from the pylon sets the bank: closer means steeper [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].
Pivotal altitude does not vary with bank unless the bank is steep enough to affect groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].
The Figure 7-12 values agree with both rules to within about 10 feet: 100 knots gives 10,000 / 11.3 = 885, and 115 mph gives 13,225 / 15 = 882 [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

callout.text: Speed squared over 11.3, plus the ground. Bank picks the circle, not the height.

check.q: Your learner wants to bank 45° instead of 30° 'so we can fly lower.' What do you tell them?
check.a: Bank does not change pivotal altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]; groundspeed does [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. A steeper bank only means flying closer to the pylon [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: What moves the pivotal altitude: wind, groundspeed and weight

body.p: Wind moves the airplane over the ground at the wind's speed no matter what the airspeed is [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Headed upwind, groundspeed is less than airspeed; headed downwind, it is more; with the wind across the nose, its effect on groundspeed is smallest [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. Because the headings run from downwind to upwind all through each turn, the pivotal altitude changes slightly throughout the turn, and the pilot climbs or descends to hold the line on the pylon [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

head: Factor
Effect on pivotal altitude
Source
rows: Groundspeed lower, pivotal altitude lower: descend
Groundspeed higher, pivotal altitude higher: climb
Wind changes groundspeed least; pivotal altitude near the no-wind value
POH maneuvering speeds vary by weight; a slower airspeed means a lower groundspeed and pivotal altitude
The rule gives height above the pylon; add its MSL elevation, found on the sectional
No change unless steep enough to affect groundspeed
Brief groundspeed changes; correct with a small temporary bank change

body.p: Eights on pylons does not require a constant radius, so no drift correction is applied in the turn [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. That is the big difference from eights around pylons, which holds a constant radius by changing bank [[24:159|AFH 7-13]]. Between the pylons the wind is corrected again: roll out with the proper wind correction angle so you arrive downwind of the second pylon as far from it as you started from the first [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

Sensitivity (computed, application): near 100 knots each knot of groundspeed is worth about 18 feet (2 x 100 / 11.3 = 17.7). With 100 knots and a 10-knot wind, the upwind value is 8,100 / 11.3 = 717 feet and the downwind value 12,100 / 11.3 = 1,071 feet: a swing of about 354 feet in every turn.

callout.text: The computed number is a starting point only. The pylon's apparent movement tells you where pivotal altitude is; trying to correct it by the altimeter is ineffective [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

check.q: Name the inputs the AFH says you can gather before flight to estimate the pivotal altitudes, and for which positions you compute them.
check.a: Wind direction and velocity, the MSL elevation of the pylons from the sectional, and the POH maneuvering airspeed for the weight; compute upwind, downwind and crosswind [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

body.p: In a bank, the horizontal component of lift turns the airplane, not the rudder [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. The rudder coordinates the turn by countering adverse yaw from the ailerons [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. To hold altitude in the turn, the pilot raises the angle of attack with back pressure and adds power for the extra drag [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

During a skid the pilot feels pressed toward the outside of the turn; during a slip, toward the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. A pilot should become sensitive to a slip or skid without leaning on the instruments [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

The trap in this maneuver: when the reference line moves forward of the pylon, many pilots apply inside rudder to yaw the wing back; when it moves behind, outside rudder to yaw it forward [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]. Inside rudder in a turn gives a skid, outside rudder a slip (application of [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]). The AFH says forcing the wing to the pylon with rudder puts the airplane in uncoordinated flight, at low altitude, with steep bank, and should not be attempted [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

bullets: Inside rudder with steep bank is the control set of the base-to-final cross-control stall: the bank increases, the nose drops, the pilot pulls, and a stall can quickly become a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can enter a spin in the direction of the rudder, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
The words to give the learner: rudder keeps the ball centered, altitude keeps the pylon [[24:164|AFH 7-18]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

callout.text: S8 reads 'Maintain pylon position using appropriate pivotal altitude, avoiding slips and skids' (ACS AI.IX.F.S8). A perfect pylon held with a skid does not meet it.

check.q: In a right turn the reference line moves ahead of the pylon. What does the rudder 'fix' look like, what does it create, and what is the real fix?
check.a: Inside (right) rudder to yaw the wing back [[24:164|AFH 7-18]], which is a skid (application of [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]). The real fix is to climb, because the line ahead of the pylon means the airplane is low [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Selecting pylons and planning the flight

bullets: Prominent enough to see while completing the turn around one pylon and heading for the next [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
Spaced for 3 to 5 seconds of straight-and-level flight between them: enough to plan the turns, not so much that it adds needless straight flight [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
At the same elevation; differences of more than a few feet mean climbing or descending between turns [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
On a line perpendicular to the wind [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

In an area away from open-air assemblies of people, congested areas and herds of livestock, with at least 500 feet vertical and 2,000 feet horizontal obstruction clearance, and with emergency landing spots available [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
When picking references, weigh the maneuver, altitude, emergency landing needs, density of structures, wind, visibility and airspace [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

body.p: Spacing in feet (computed): at 95 knots the airplane covers 95 x 1.69 = 160.6 feet per second [[1:137|PHAK 5-40]], so 3 to 5 seconds is about 480 to 800 feet of straight flight between the turns.

Many instructors already have pylons picked out [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Even so, let the learner choose them on some flights: the AIH suggests prompting the learner, before a ground reference maneuver, to name potential collision hazards and a safe place for an emergency landing [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Their choice shows you whether they understand wind, spacing and elevation.

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.119: anywhere, an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard if the engine fails; over other than congested areas, 500 feet above the surface, and over sparsely populated areas no closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. A barn or silo used as a pylon is a structure.

check.q: Your learner picks a grain bin and a farmhouse about a mile apart, lined up with the wind. Name two problems.
check.a: They lie along the wind instead of perpendicular to it, and they are far more than 3 to 5 seconds of straight flight apart [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. The farmhouse is also a structure you must stay at least 500 feet from [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

chunks.title: Flying the eight: entry to recovery

head: Phase
What the pilot does
Source
rows: Estimate pivotal altitudes; look up the POH stall speed at 50° or the steepest bank expected
Checklist, practice-area radio call, two 90° clearing turns looking left, right, above and below
The demonstration from below and above pivotal altitude, then a descending turn until the line stops
Diagonally crosswind between the pylons to a point downwind of the first pylon, so the first turn is into the wind; no faster than maneuvering speed
As the pylon appears just ahead of the wingtip, lower the upwind wing until the reference line aligns with the pylon
Groundspeed drops, pivotal altitude lowers: descend
Groundspeed builds: climb, adding power to hold airspeed
Head diagonally to a point tangent on the downwind side of the second pylon, with a wind correction angle
Turn the opposite way, flown like the first
No source gives one (see gaps). Application: roll out between the pylons, return to the briefed altitude and airspeed, and clear

body.p: Corrections come in two kinds. A line that keeps drifting ahead of the pylon means you are low, so climb; drifting behind means high, so descend [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. For brief variations from gusts or inattention, shallow the bank slightly to bring a lagging line forward, or steepen it briefly to turn back a line that has moved ahead [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. With prompt correction and very fine control pressures the line can be held on the pylon even in strong wind [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

Banks range from shallow to steep. As proficiency builds, the instructor directs an entry distance that gives a specific bank at the steepest point [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. The Task caps it at 40° (ACS AI.IX.F.S5), tighter than the AFH's general note of 45° and maneuvering speed for ground reference maneuvers [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

check.q: Where does the first turn begin, and which way is it relative to the wind?
check.a: From a diagonal crosswind entry to a point downwind of the first pylon, so the first turn is into the wind [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

body.p: Build it from blocks. Ground reference maneuvers start once the learner is proficient in the four fundamentals [[24:147|AFH 7-1]], and eights on pylons comes last: it reuses the groundspeed and drift lessons of turns around a point and eights around pylons [[24:154|AFH 7-8]] [[24:159|AFH 7-13]]. When a new maneuver relates to ones already learned, the AIH suggests known to unknown [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]: 'This is your eight around pylons, except now the circle is free and the altitude moves.'

On the ground, give the objective and standard, the actions and the end result, and the safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. For this maneuver that means: the line of sight (not the wingtip), today's pivotal altitude estimates for upwind, crosswind and downwind [[24:162|AFH 7-16]], what each direction of pylon movement means [[24:163|AFH 7-17]], rudder only for coordination [[24:164|AFH 7-18]], the 40° limit (ACS AI.IX.F.S5), the emergency field, and how you will exchange controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

Use the AFH's built-in demonstration. At maneuvering speed below pivotal altitude, in a medium bank, show the line moving forward along the ground (pylon moving back). Climb well above, and show it moving backward (pylon moving forward). Then reduce power and descend at maneuvering speed in the continuing medium-bank turn: the backward movement slows and stops for an instant. That altitude is the pivotal altitude [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. It turns a formula into something the learner can see.

head: Moment
Sample patter (application)
Basis
rows: 'We are low. Watch the line run ahead along the ground; the pylon slides back.'
'Now we are high. The line slides backward; the pylon creeps ahead.'
'Power back, same airspeed. The movement slows, slows, stops. That is pivotal altitude for this groundspeed.'
'Groundspeed is dropping, so I ease down to keep the line on it.'
'Groundspeed is building. Climb, with a little power to hold the speed.'
'Wind correction angle, aiming downwind of the next pylon, same distance as before.'

bullets: Have the learner call the climbs and descents while you fly; you hear whether they read the line or the altimeter [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Make the first eights correct ones; never let the first pylon turns be held with rudder, because what is learned first sticks [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

Once it is flown well, vary it: direct a specific bank at the steepest point through the entry distance [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. If you suspect they fly it by rote without understanding it, have them vary it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Low: line runs ahead, pylon slides back, climb. High: line slides back, pylon runs ahead, descend.

check.q: What does the AFH have you demonstrate before the first full eight, and what does the learner see?
check.a: Turns below and well above pivotal altitude (line moving forward, then backward), then a descending turn in which the line's movement slows and stops for an instant at pivotal altitude [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

body.p: On the practical test you demonstrate and explain at the same time (ACS AI.IX.F Skills). That is the 'instructor tells, instructor does' step: the demonstration must match the explanation, in the same order, and be flown exactly the way you want it practiced, safety procedures included [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

bullets: If the demonstration strays from what you explained, say so at once and explain why [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

Your reference line is from your seat. In side-by-side airplanes it differs little from the learner's when your eyes are at about the same level [[24:160|AFH 7-14]]; check yours from the right seat before the checkride.

The AFH notes the lowered high wing may hide the point in a left turn from the left seat [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. Application: from the right seat the same may happen in right turns, so check your view of the pylon in both directions before the checkride.
Use plain words and avoid jargon the learner does not know [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Exchange controls positively before and after; when the learner flies, guard the controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Keep clearing aloud during your demonstration: the lookout is shared, and learners who think the instructor does it all never build the habit [[25:191|AIH 10-7]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Fly your demonstration to the standard you will grade: ball centered, steepest bank at or below 40°, line on the pylon (ACS AI.IX.F.S5, S6, S8). Name each correction as you make it: 'Line moving ahead, climbing a little.'

check.q: During your demonstration a gust carries the line ahead of the pylon for a moment. What do you do and say?
check.a: Acknowledge the deviation right away [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], then explain the fix as you make it: steepen the bank briefly to turn the line back [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Energy management: power, airspeed and altitude

body.p: Energy management is planning, monitoring and controlling altitude and airspeed, and getting it wrong contributes to loss of control, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. The pilot's frame of reference is the airplane's own: indicated altitude and indicated airspeed, not height above ground or groundspeed [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Eights on pylons is unusual because its target, pivotal altitude, is set by groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]], which the pilot cannot change directly [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

bullets: Climbing without added energy trades airspeed for altitude [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. The AFH has the pilot increase power to maintain airspeed while regaining altitude [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
Lost airspeed lowers groundspeed and so the pivotal altitude; the learner ends up chasing a moving target (application of [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]).
Holding altitude in a turn takes more angle of attack, and power for the added drag [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Look up the POH stall speed at 50° or the steepest bank expected [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Stay at or below maneuvering speed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], which the POH gives by weight [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

callout.text: Watch for the learner who pulls to climb on the downwind side and lets the speed decay while banked: the margin above the higher stall speed in the turn shrinks, and it is happening low [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

check.q: Why does the AFH have the pilot add power when climbing back up to pivotal altitude?
check.a: To maintain airspeed while regaining altitude [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]; without added energy the climb comes out of airspeed [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

chunks.title: Low altitude: stall, spin and CFIT

body.p: Ground reference maneuvers put the airplane low, where the hazards include other aircraft (helicopters too), towers and wires, and engine failure [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. They are generally flown between 600 and 1,000 feet AGL [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and pivotal altitudes often land near that band: 95 knots gives 9,025 / 11.3 = 799 feet above the pylon (computed).

bullets: Keep at least 500 feet vertical and 2,000 feet horizontal clearance from obstructions [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
The lower the altitude, the faster the airplane seems to move over the ground, and an engine failure leaves less time and glide distance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
An accelerated stall in a steep turn can surprise the pilot, and failing to recover at once can lead to a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
The skidding cross-control stall gives little warning and can be deadly close to the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
If the yaw came from wrong rudder, the pilot may not notice the critical angle of attack is exceeded until the airplane yaws out of control toward the lowering wing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
Mismanaged energy is a factor in CFIT [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]; here that is a learner who keeps descending to chase the pylon. Set a floor before the flight (application).

callout.text: Set your limits on the ground: a floor, the 40° bank cap and a centered ball. If the learner breaks them, take the airplane and say 'I have the flight controls.' Learners should never be allowed to exceed the instructor's limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Why is a learner who holds the pylon with inside rudder more dangerous than one who simply loses the pylon?
check.a: The skid at low altitude and steep bank is the cross-control stall setup, with little warning and a possible roll toward inverted [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]; a stall while skidding can spin in the direction of the rudder [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

chunks.title: Collision hazards and emergency landing options

body.p: In the AIH's midair study, flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of the accidents, the vast majority happened at or near nontowered airports and below 1,000 feet, and most happened in daylight with visibility over 3 miles [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. That is exactly where ground reference maneuvers are flown [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

bullets: Clear with two 90° turns looking left, right, above and below [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and have the learner say it aloud: 'clear left, right, above and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Teach one clearing procedure and insist on it [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Move your head and, when needed, lift a wing to see around blind spots such as the wing and door posts [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
An aircraft with no relative motion that stays in one scan quadrant is likely on a collision course; expect the other pilot to maneuver too, and resume scanning afterward [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Both of you are responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
Have one or more emergency landing spots picked before entry [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and prompt the learner to name them [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

Land into the wind if you can: doubling the groundspeed at touchdown quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. Excess airspeed can be turned into distance or altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

callout.text: Make the forced landing field the 'third pylon' (application): before entry the learner points to it and says which way they would land on it, given today's wind [[25:192|AIH 10-8]] [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

check.q: What did the AIH midair study find about altitude and location?
check.a: The vast majority occurred at or near nontowered airports and below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], the same band where ground reference maneuvers are generally flown [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

chunks.title: Division of attention, distraction and orientation

body.p: Ground reference maneuvers develop division of attention: hold attitude, track the reference, scan for other aircraft, prepare for an emergency landing, and scan the flight and engine instruments at regular intervals [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]. Eights on pylons asks the most of it, because the reference is a single point beside you [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

bullets: Fixing the eyes on one reference loses the sense of rate; scan across several references [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].
Fixation is absorption in one task to the exclusion of others; inattention often follows it [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].
Follow the learner's eyes: a long stare at one spot suggests fixation, and a gaze that never reaches the engine instruments suggests inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].
Before combining tasks, the learner should do each one reasonably well alone [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. If they cannot hold a pylon and scan, go back a block.
Situational awareness covers aircraft position, flight path, other aircraft and the environment; when busy, budget time and prioritize [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
Practice distractions on purpose. AIH examples that fit here: identify objects on the ground, or a field suitable for a forced landing [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

Disorientation: after several turns learners lose track of the wind and which pylon is next. 'Failure to maintain orientation' is a listed error for the eights around pylons that come before this maneuver [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

callout.text: Pylon, horizon, ball, traffic, engine, field. Then the pylon again.

check.q: Your learner holds the pylon well, but the head never moves and the eyes never go to the engine gauges. What is it, and how did you spot it?
check.a: Fixation on the pylon with inattention to the rest, spotted by following the learner's eyes [[25:82|AIH 3-31]] [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

body.p: The AFH calls incorrect rudder use the most common error in holding a pylon and lists nine more [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]. For S9 the evaluator will fly some of them; name what you see, explain the cause, and give the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Line ahead of the pylon: inside rudder; line behind: outside rudder. Pylon steady, ball out
Rudder only for coordination [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]; fix the line with altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
Failure to clear the area, initially and throughout
No clearing turns, no look below, head still once turning
Two 90° clearing turns and a scan throughout [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]
Ball off center, pilot pushed sideways, with or without chasing the pylon
Coordinated aileron and rudder; teach the feel [[24:74|AFH 3-13]] [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]
Excessive gain or loss of altitude
The proper pivotal altitude varies only slightly through the turn [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]; small, early corrections
Not prominent, too far apart, different elevations, not across the wind
Not entering the pylon turns into the wind
Diagonal crosswind entry to a point downwind of the first pylon [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
No heading between pylons that compensates for drift
Arrives too close to or too far from the second pylon
Wind correction angle, aiming downwind of the second pylon at the same distance [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
Bank not timed so the entry is complete with the pylon in position
Rolls in late with the pylon already behind, or early
Start the roll as the pylon appears just ahead of the wingtip [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
Prompt correction with very fine control pressures [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
Flies the altimeter number while the line wanders
Read the line, not the altimeter [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]; fly the below-and-above demonstration again [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]

body.p: How to analyze it: having the learner think aloud shows whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, it is often better to let learners go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], but a skid in a steep, low bank is one to stop early [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. If it needs reteaching, demonstrate again, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Read the ball and the pylon together. Pylon steady with the ball out means the rudder is doing the altitude's job [[24:164|AFH 7-18]].

check.q: As your learner, the examiner keeps the pylon in place on the downwind side, but the altitude barely changes and the ball sits to the outside of the turn. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Holding the pylon with inside rudder, the most common error [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]. Fix: rudder only to center the ball, and climb as groundspeed builds [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

f1.caption: Figure 7-10. Eights on pylons. (AFH 7-14)
f1.alt: Top view of a figure eight flown over farmland around two red dot pylons, with a blue wind arrow pointing down the page. An entry path comes in from the upper left. Dashed red lines run from each pylon to the airplanes around the loops. Labels mark gaining altitude on the upper part of each loop, high groundspeed and high pivotal altitude near the bottom, and lowest groundspeed and lowest pivotal altitude at the far right side.

f2.caption: Figure 7-11. Line of sight. (AFH 7-15)
f2.alt: Two drawings of an airplane, one from above and one banked, show the line of sight from the pilot's eyes running parallel to the lateral axis along the wing. Two cockpit photos use a pond as the pylon: one labeled too high, pylon ahead, and one labeled too low, pylon behind.

f3.caption: Figure 7-12. Speed versus pivotal altitude. (AFH 7-15)
f3.alt: A table of groundspeed in knots and mph against approximate pivotal altitude: 87 knots or 100 mph, 670; 91 or 105, 735; 96 or 110, 810; 100 or 115, 885; 104 or 120, 960; 109 or 125, 1,050; 113 or 130, 1,130.

f4.caption: Figure 7-13. Effect of different altitudes on line of sight. (AFH 7-16)
f4.alt: Three banked airplanes circle a tower pylon on stacked rings labeled too high, pivotal altitude and too low. A sight line from each airplane runs to the ground: from the middle one it meets the pylon, from the top one it lands beyond it, and from the bottom one it falls short of it.

f5.caption: Figure 7-14. Bank angle versus pivotal altitude. (AFH 7-17)
f5.alt: Side view of a tower pylon and three airplanes on one horizontal line marked pivotal altitude. Red sight lines run along each airplane's lowered wing to the pylon. The airplane closest to the pylon is banked 60°, the middle one 45° and the farthest one 30°.

f6.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid. (AFH 3-13)
f6.alt: Three panels: skid, coordinated turn and slip. Each shows an attitude indicator in a right bank, a turn coordinator and a seat with a red arrow. In the skid the ball is to the outside of the turn and the pilot feels pushed outward; coordinated, the ball is centered and the force is straight down into the seat; in the slip the ball is to the inside and the pilot feels pushed inward.

f7.caption: Figure 5-15. Spin, an aggravated stall and autorotation. (AFH 5-22)
f7.alt: An airplane, nose down and banked, rotating around a tall vertical pole while following a ribbon that corkscrews down around the pole against a blue sky.

scenario.title: Strong wind, a learner who holds it with rudder
scenario.setup: You are a CFI with a commercial learner in a four-seat high-wing trainer. The wind at 1,000 feet is from the west at about 18 knots. The practice area is farmland at 1,200 feet MSL with two silos on a north-south line, a few houses, and a helicopter that sprays the fields. The POH maneuvering speed for today's weight is 95 knots. Last lesson the learner held every pylon with rudder.

questions.q: The learner plans 95 knots. What pivotal altitudes do you brief for crosswind, upwind and downwind?
questions.a: Crosswind about 95 knots: 9,025 / 11.3 = 799 feet, about 2,000 feet MSL. Upwind 77 knots: 5,929 / 11.3 = 525 feet, about 1,725 MSL. Downwind 113 knots: 12,769 / 11.3 = 1,130 feet, about 2,330 MSL [[24:161|AFH 7-15]] [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. They are estimates; the line on the pylon decides [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

questions.q: What does that 525-foot upwind number make you think about?
questions.a: It sits below the AFH's usual 600 to 1,000 feet AGL band and leaves little time or glide distance if the engine quits [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Over sparsely populated land you must still stay 500 feet from any person, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. At 95 knots you are already at maneuvering speed, the general limit [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], so flying faster is not the answer. Choose a lighter-wind day, or brief a higher floor and stop the maneuver if the upwind side gets too low (application).

questions.q: Before entry the helicopter appears low over a field two miles away. What do you do and teach?
questions.a: The AFH says to look for other aircraft, including helicopters, at these altitudes [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Clear with two 90° turns, make the practice-area call [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and keep it in sight: one with no relative motion that grows is a collision threat [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Remind the learner the lookout is shared [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: On the first upwind turn the learner holds altitude and presses inside rudder; the ball goes to the outside. Do you let it develop?
questions.a: No. Yawing the wing to the pylon at low altitude and steep bank should not be attempted [[24:163|AFH 7-17]], and a stall while skidding can spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Coach 'ball centered, ease down', since upwind the pivotal altitude is lower [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. If it continues past your limits, take the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], then fly the below-and-above demonstration again [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

questions.q: Later the learner's altitude swings 300 feet each turn and the eyes stay on the altimeter. What is going on, and what distraction might you add once it is fixed?
questions.a: Fixation on the altimeter [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]; correcting pivotal altitude by the altimeter is ineffective [[24:163|AFH 7-17]], so teach the line first. Once stable, add a distraction that fits: ask for a field suitable for a forced landing [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

questions.q: On the downwind side at about 1,100 feet AGL the engine runs rough and loses power. What is the plan?
questions.a: Fly to the field picked before entry [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], using the extra airspeed for distance or altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Plan to land into the west wind: groundspeed at touchdown governs the energy, and doubling it quadruples the energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

skills.do: Clear the area before entry and throughout while explaining it: checklist, practice-area radio call, two 90° clearing turns looking left, right, above and below.
skills.practice: Call your clearing aloud before every ground reference maneuver and keep scanning between the pylons [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Determine the approximate pivotal altitude: groundspeed squared over 11.3 (knots) plus the pylon's MSL, for upwind, crosswind and downwind, then explain how you find the real one by the line.
skills.practice: Before each flight, compute the three values from the winds aloft, the sectional and the POH maneuvering speed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]] [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

skills.do: Select suitable pylons that permit straight-and-level flight between them, and say why: prominent, same elevation, 3 to 5 seconds apart, on a line perpendicular to the wind, away from people and livestock.
skills.practice: Keep a list of pylon pairs for several wind directions in your practice area [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

skills.do: Enter in the correct direction and position at an appropriate altitude and airspeed: diagonally crosswind to a point downwind of the first pylon, first turn into the wind, at no more than maneuvering speed.
skills.practice: Fly entries until you roll in with the pylon just ahead of the wingtip every time [[24:163|AFH 7-17]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

skills.do: Establish the correct bank angle for the conditions, not to exceed 40° (ACS AI.IX.F.S5), and explain that entry distance, not altitude, sets the bank.
skills.practice: Have a safety pilot call your steepest bank; adjust entry distance until it stays at or below 40° [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

skills.do: Apply smooth and continuous corrections so the line-of-sight reference line remains on the pylon, naming each correction: altitude for a drifting line, a brief bank change for a gust.
skills.practice: Fly eights while saying 'line ahead, climb' or 'line behind, descend' aloud [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

skills.do: Divide attention between accurate, coordinated control and outside references while talking: pylon, horizon, ball, traffic, engine gauges, emergency field.
skills.practice: Fly eights with a friend watching your eyes and calling when you fixate [[24:147|AFH 7-1]] [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

skills.do: Maintain pylon position using the appropriate pivotal altitude with the ball centered, avoiding slips and skids.
skills.practice: Fly with your feet doing only coordination and glance at the ball at each quarter turn [[24:164|AFH 7-18]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

skills.do: Watch the evaluator, acting as learner, fly errors such as rudder holding, late roll-in or no wind correction between pylons; name each one, explain its cause and teach the fix.
skills.practice: Have another instructor applicant fly the AFH error list at you and practice spotting each one [[24:164|AFH 7-18]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

quiz.q: Which reference does the AFH say some instructors use for the visual reference line, and calls not correct?
options: The wing strut
The lateral axis
The wingtip
The cowling edge
quiz.why: Instructors sometimes use 'wingtip' for the reference line; the AFH says this interpretation is not correct [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: In a side-by-side airplane, when does the AFH say the visual reference lines of two pilots vary little?
options: When their eyes are at about the same level
When both pilots sight along the wingtip as the reference
When the airplane is a low-wing design
When the bank is kept shallow
quiz.why: In side-by-side airplanes there is very little variation if the pilots' eyes are at approximately the same level [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: From the left seat of a high-wing, side-by-side airplane, when does the AFH warn that the lowered wing may hide your ground reference?
options: In right turns, when the right wing is lowered
Only when flying below about 600 feet AGL
Only in tandem-seat airplanes with a high wing
In left turns, when the left wing is lowered
quiz.why: The AFH gives this warning in its turns around a point section: the lowered wing may block the view, especially in a left turn with the pilot in the left seat [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. Check that the pylon stays in view before you teach eights on pylons.

quiz.q: Where does the AFH say you find the MSL elevation of known pylons, to add to the rule-of-thumb height?
options: The airport field elevation in the Chart Supplement
The sectional chart
The altimeter reading on the ground before takeoff
The performance section of the POH
quiz.why: If the references are already known, the sectional chart gives their MSL elevation; the POH gives the maneuvering speeds [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. The rule adds the MSL altitude of the reference [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say about yawing the wing back onto the pylon with rudder?
options: It is fine for small corrections, as long as the ball returns to center afterward
It is the preferred fix for brief gusts, because it does not change the altitude
It should not be attempted: it means uncoordinated flight, low, in a steep bank
It is allowed only above 1,000 feet AGL, where there is room to recover from a stall
quiz.why: Deflecting the rudder to force the wing and reference line to the pylon places the airplane in uncoordinated flight, at low altitude, with steep bank, and should not be attempted [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Gusts are handled with a brief bank change [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

quiz.q: Which skill element appears in the CFI Task but not in the commercial one?
options: S9, analyze and correct common errors
S5, bank not to exceed 40°
S3, select suitable pylons
S8, maintain pylon position avoiding slips and skids
quiz.why: The CFI Task adds S9 (ACS AI.IX.F.S9); S1 to S8 match the commercial wording (ACS CA.V.E.S1 to S8).

quiz.q: During preflight planning, which stall speed does AFH 7-2 tell you to determine?
options: The clean wings-level stall speed at the maximum certificated weight
The stall speed with full flaps at idle power
The accelerated stall speed at maneuvering speed
The POH stall speed at 50° or the steepest bank expected
quiz.why: Determine the predicted (POH/AFM) stall speed at 50° or the highest bank expected, to keep a margin [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

quiz.q: How does the AFH say eights on pylons differs from the earlier ground-track maneuvers?
options: The pilot holds a constant radius by changing bank instead of altitude
The pilot holds a lateral relationship to one spot, not a set path over the ground
The pilot holds a fixed altitude and corrects for drift all through each turn
The pilot uses the altimeter, not ground references, as the main reference
quiz.why: In the earlier ground-track maneuvers the airplane flies a set path over the ground; in eights on pylons the pilot maintains lateral orientation to a specific spot [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

quiz.q: Your learner says the rudder is what turns the airplane around the pylon. What does the AFH say turns it?
options: The rudder, with the ailerons used only to hold the bank
Added power, which pulls the nose around toward the pylon
The horizontal component of lift from the banked wing
Adverse yaw from the down aileron on the rising wing
quiz.why: It is the horizontal lift component that turns the airplane, not the rudder; the rudder coordinates the turn [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

quiz.q: Which midair study finding in the AIH matters most for ground reference practice?
options: Most happened at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet
Most happened in haze, smoke or rain with visibility below 3 miles
Most involved aircraft on IFR flight plans with ATC
Most involved pilots on their first solo flights
quiz.why: The vast majority occurred at or near nontowered airports and below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], where these maneuvers are flown [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: Crosswind groundspeed 92 knots, pylons at 860 feet MSL. Your learner briefs 'pivotal altitude 749' and plans to hold 749 on the altimeter. What do you say?
options: Correct: the rule of thumb already gives an altimeter reading in feet MSL
Wrong divisor: with knots use 15, so the target is about 1,424 feet MSL
Subtract the elevation instead, so the altimeter target is about 111 feet
Add the pylon elevation: 749 + 860 gives a target of about 1,609 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: 92 x 92 = 8,464. 8,464 / 11.3 = 749 feet above the pylons; then add the MSL elevation of the reference: 749 + 860 = 1,609 feet MSL [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. 15 is the divisor for mph, not knots.

final_quiz.q: Your learner is much taller than you. What should you expect when you teach the reference line?
options: The learner's line will match yours, since both seats face forward the same way
Their line crosses the wing at a different spot; teach the eye line
The learner should use the wingtip, since height differences cancel out in a bank
The learner should copy your strut landmark so you can check each other easily
final_quiz.why: The line differs for each pilot; variation is small only when eyes are at about the same level [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

final_quiz.q: How do you teach your learner to choose between an altitude change and a bank change when the line moves?
options: Altitude on upwind headings and bank on downwind headings, every time
Bank for any movement at all, since the altitude is set before entry
Altitude for a line that keeps moving; a brief bank change for a gust or lapse
Altitude for any movement, since any bank change causes a slip or a skid
final_quiz.why: A line that keeps moving ahead or behind calls for a climb or descent; temporary variations from gusts or inattention are fixed by briefly changing the bank [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: The learner finishes rolling in with the pylon already well behind the reference line. Which listed error is it, and the fix?
options: Entry not timed to the pylon; start rolling as it appears just ahead of the wingtip
Poor choice of pylons; pick pylons farther apart so there is more time to complete the roll-in
Not entering into the wind; enter from the upwind side of the first pylon instead
Abrupt control use; roll in more slowly and let the pylon come back to you
final_quiz.why: Failure to time the bank so the entry is completed with the pylon in position is listed [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]; begin the turn as the pylon appears just ahead of the wingtip [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: As your learner, the examiner flies a smooth eight but makes no clearing turns before entry and never looks above or below the wings. What do you name, and the fix?
options: Poor choice of pylons; pick pylons away from traffic so clearing is not needed
Abrupt control usage; smoother inputs leave more time to look outside
Not entering into the wind; a correct entry gives a clear view of the area
Failure to clear the area; two 90° clearing turns and a scan throughout
final_quiz.why: Failure to adequately clear the area, initially and throughout, is a listed error [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]. Clear with two 90° turns looking left, right, above and below [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner holds the line perfectly using 45° at the steepest point. Which element is not met?
options: S8, because the pivotal altitude must change with bank
S5, because the bank is not to exceed 40°
S6, because the corrections were not continuous
S3, because the pylons must be closer together
final_quiz.why: S5: 'Establish the correct bank angle for the conditions, not to exceed 40°' (ACS AI.IX.F.S5). Bank does not change pivotal altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants to fly 115 knots, above the 105-knot POH maneuvering speed, to raise the pivotal altitude over some trees. Your answer?
options: Fine, since a higher pivotal altitude gives better obstacle clearance
Fine, if the bank stays below 30° the whole way around
No: stay at or below maneuvering speed and pick different pylons
No: instead fly 115 knots but cap the bank at 20°
final_quiz.why: As a general note, ground reference maneuvers should not exceed maneuvering speed, and pylons should allow obstruction clearance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: Rolling into a steep left pylon turn in a high-wing airplane, how does the AIM suggest you see around fixed blind spots?
options: Move your head, and at times maneuver, such as lifting a wing
Rely on the two clearing turns you flew before starting the maneuver
Ask ATC for traffic advisories and stop scanning
Lower the nose to look over the cowling
final_quiz.why: Pilots need to move their heads to see around blind spots such as wings and door posts, and at times maneuver, e.g. lift a wing [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

final_quiz.q: The engine fails on the downwind side. One field lies ahead downwind and one behind you, landing into the wind. Both are reachable. Which and why?
options: The downwind field, because the tailwind stretches the glide to reach it
Either one, since touchdown energy depends only on the airspeed
The field ahead, because turning at low altitude is never acceptable
The into-wind field, because a lower groundspeed sharply cuts the touchdown energy
final_quiz.why: Doubling the groundspeed quadruples the destructive energy, so a lower groundspeed at touchdown matters most [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. Excess airspeed can be traded for distance [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

final_quiz.q: For three eights your learner holds the pylon well but never glances at the engine gauges or the sky. Which AIH problem is it, and the first defense?
options: Overconfidence; give a harder version of the maneuver to rebuild their focus
Inattention; alert the learner and build habits that keep attention spread
Lack of motor skill; return to straight-and-level
Fatigue; end the lesson immediately
final_quiz.why: A gaze that never reaches the engine instruments suggests inattention; the first defense is to alert the learner and build habits [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

final_quiz.q: Which AIH distraction fits most naturally into eights on pylons practice?
options: Ask the learner to fetch something from the back seat
Ask the learner to compute true airspeed with a computer
Ask the learner to identify a field suitable for a forced landing
Ask the learner to reset the clock on the panel
final_quiz.why: The AIH list includes identifying a field suitable for a forced landing [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], which also serves the low-altitude emergency plan [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies good eights but you suspect they memorized the pattern. What variation does the AFH suggest for this maneuver?
options: Direct an entry distance that gives a specific bank at the steepest point
Fly the eight at 300 feet lower than the pivotal altitude
Have them hold the pylon with rudder to feel the difference
Switch to pylons a mile apart to lengthen the straight leg
final_quiz.why: The instructor should increase complexity by directing an entry distance that gives a specific bank at the steepest point [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]; if you suspect a learner flies it without understanding it, the AIH says to have them vary it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: A learner computes pivotal altitude for 100 knots as 10,000 / 15 = 667 feet. What is wrong, and by how much?
options: Nothing; 15 is the divisor for knots and 11.3 for mph
The groundspeed should be squared twice; it is far too low
The pylon elevation was added twice, so it is too high
The mph divisor was used with knots; it is about 218 feet too low
final_quiz.why: Divide by 11.3 for knots and 15 for mph [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. 10,000 / 11.3 = 885; 885 - 667 = 218 feet too low.

takeaways: Purpose: hold one spot with a line from your eyes along the lateral axis, not the wingtip, while dividing attention.
Pivotal altitude = groundspeed squared / 11.3 (knots) plus pylon elevation. Bank does not change it; groundspeed does.
Upwind: groundspeed drops, descend. Downwind: it builds, climb with power. The line, not the altimeter, is the truth.
Line ahead of the pylon: climb. Line behind: descend. Gusts: a brief bank change.
Rudder only coordinates. Holding the pylon with rudder is the most common error and a low-altitude stall/spin setup.
Pylons: prominent, same elevation, 3 to 5 seconds apart, across the wind, away from people and livestock. Bank never past 40°.
Teach with the AFH below-and-above demonstration, fly your demo to standard, and watch the learner's eyes and the ball.
cfi_notes: Skills S1 to S8 of the CFI Task match the commercial wording (ACS CA.V.E.S1 to S8). The CFI Task adds K6 and S9, common errors, and 'procedures' in K1 (ACS AI.IX.F.K1, K6, S9).

The AFH says outright that the 'wingtip' reference is not correct [[24:160|AFH 7-14]], yet many pilots learned it that way. Correct it gently and replace it with the lateral axis line from the learner's own eyes.

The AFH gives two corrections: altitude for a line that keeps moving ahead or behind, and a brief bank change for temporary variations from gusts or inattention [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Teach which is which, or learners mix them.

The AFH divisor is 11.3 [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]; the PHAK radius formula uses 11.26 [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. Both describe the same geometry (application), and Figure 7-12's values match either rule within about 10 feet. Do not argue decimals with a learner.
The AFH's general note allows 45° for ground reference maneuvers [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]; this Task caps it at 40° (ACS AI.IX.F.S5). Teach 40°.

The AFH's usual 600 to 1,000 feet AGL band [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] does not set the altitude here; groundspeed does [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. In strong wind the upwind pivotal altitude can fall below 600 feet AGL. Check 14 CFR 91.119 [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]] and consider a lighter-wind day.

The AFH explains the hidden pylon only for left turns from the left seat in a high wing [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. From the right seat it may happen in right turns instead (application); check your view of the pylon both ways before you demonstrate.

The AIH's 'let the learner go part way into the mistake' [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] has a hard limit here: the AFH says yawing the wing to the pylon at low altitude with steep bank should not be attempted [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Stop rudder holding early.
The AFH below-and-above demonstration [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] costs altitude and a few minutes; budget both in the lesson plan so it is not skipped.
gaps: No source gives an exit or recovery procedure for eights on pylons, although ACS K5 says 'from entry to recovery'; the AFH ends with the second turn [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Brief your own.
The ACS gives no altitude tolerance and no number of eights; only the 40° bank cap (ACS AI.IX.F.S5). Agree on the rest with your learner and the evaluator.
No source says what airspeed within the maneuvering speed range to fly, or whether to use flaps; use the POH/AFM [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
The AFH gives pylon spacing only in seconds (3 to 5) [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]; no source gives it in feet or says how far the line may move before it counts as an error.
The sources do not cover how a low wing or a right-seat view changes what the pylon looks like; check it in your own airplane before you teach it.

activities.title: Higher, lower or no change?
activities.intro: Tap a change, then tap what it does to the pivotal altitude.

items.t: The headwind on the upwind heading grows from 10 to 20 knots
The wind dies away while you are heading upwind
Choosing pylons on ground 200 feet higher (altimeter target)
The tailwind on the downwind heading grows stronger
Choosing pylons on ground 150 feet lower (altimeter target)
Working the rule in mph (divide by 15) instead of knots (11.3)

activities.title: The numbers behind the pylons
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: At 95 knots airspeed, how strong a headwind on the upwind heading brings the pivotal altitude down to 600 feet above the pylon, the bottom of the AFH's usual 600 to 1,000 feet AGL band?
items.why: Groundspeed squared = 600 x 11.3 = 6,780. Square root of 6,780 = 82.3 knots. 95 - 82.3 = 12.7 knots of headwind [[24:161|AFH 7-15]] [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. In a stronger wind the upwind side sits below the usual band [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

items.q: A gust drops your groundspeed from 100 to 95 knots. How far below the old pivotal altitude is the new one?
items.why: 10,000 / 11.3 = 885.0. 9,025 / 11.3 = 798.7. 885.0 - 798.7 = 86 feet [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. For a brief gust the AFH uses a small bank change instead of chasing it [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

items.q: Your POH maneuvering speed is 99 knots at gross weight and 89 knots light. On a crosswind heading (groundspeed about equal to airspeed), how much lower is the pivotal altitude when light?
items.why: 99 x 99 / 11.3 = 867.3. 89 x 89 / 11.3 = 701.0. 867.3 - 701.0 = 166 feet [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. The POH gives maneuvering speeds by weight [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]; crosswind changes groundspeed least [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

items.q: At 95 knots groundspeed, how many feet of straight-and-level flight does a 5-second leg between the pylons cover?
items.why: 95 x 1.69 = 160.6 feet per second [[1:137|PHAK 5-40]]. 160.6 x 5 = 803 feet, the long end of the 3 to 5 seconds the AFH recommends [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

activities.title: Show the learner where pivotal altitude is
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the AFH demonstration in order, then tap Check.
steps: At maneuvering speed below pivotal altitude, roll into a medium-bank turn around the pylon
Point out the line moving forward along the ground while the pylon appears to move back
Climb well above pivotal altitude and return to maneuvering speed
In a medium-bank turn, point out the line moving backward and the pylon moving forward
Reduce power and descend at maneuvering speed in the continuing turn
Note the altitude where the line's movement stops for an instant
If you sink below it, add power and climb until the line pivots on the pylon

activities.title: What you see, what it means
activities.intro: Tap what you see from the right seat, then what it tells you.

pairs.l: Pylon steady, ball to the outside of the turn
pairs.r: Inside rudder is holding the pylon: a skid

pairs.l: Pylon steady, ball to the inside of the turn
pairs.r: Outside rudder is holding the pylon: a slip

pairs.l: Eyes on the altimeter, altitude swinging widely
pairs.r: Chasing a number; the line, not the altimeter, shows pivotal altitude

pairs.l: Large, jerky inputs every time the line moves
pairs.r: Abrupt control usage; prompt correction with very fine pressures

pairs.l: Ball centered, pylon steady, altitude easing up and down
pairs.r: Correct: altitude, not rudder, is holding the pylon

activities.title: True or false: low and close to things
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In the AIH midair study, flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of the accidents.
As a general note, the AFH says ground reference maneuvers should not exceed 45° of bank or maneuvering speed.
cards.why: True [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. This Task is stricter: not to exceed 40° (ACS AI.IX.F.S5).

cards.s: Over a sparsely populated area, 14 CFR 91.119 lets you pass 200 feet from a barn if you are 500 feet above the surface.
cards.why: False. There you may not operate closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

cards.s: An aircraft that shows no relative motion and stays in one scan quadrant is likely on a collision course.
cards.why: True [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Watch it during your avoiding maneuver, then resume the scan.

cards.s: Most stall/spin accidents in the NTSB data happened during intentional stall practice.
cards.why: False. Intentional practice seldom led to accidents; the danger was inadvertent stalls induced by distraction [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

cards.s: Dirty or bug-smeared windshields can greatly reduce your ability to see other aircraft.
Learners should never be allowed to exceed the flight instructor's limits.

activities.title: Teaching eights on pylons, one call at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFI. Your commercial learner flies a high-wing trainer. The wind at 1,000 feet is from the south at 12 knots, the farmland is at 650 feet MSL, and the POH maneuvering speed for today's weight is 95 knots.

steps.s: On the ground the learner briefs only the crosswind number, about 1,450 feet MSL. What upwind altimeter target do you have them add?
options: About 1,260 feet MSL
About 1,450 feet MSL, since it does not change upwind
About 1,660 feet MSL
About 610 feet MSL
steps.why: Upwind groundspeed 95 - 12 = 83 knots. 83 x 83 = 6,889. 6,889 / 11.3 = 609.6 feet. 609.6 + 650 = 1,259.6, about 1,260 feet MSL [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. Compute upwind, downwind and crosswind values [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. 1,660 is the downwind value; 610 leaves out the elevation.

steps.s: You fly the first eight. How do you find out whether the learner reads the line or the altimeter?
options: Fly the eight in silence and ask about it on the ground afterward
Have the learner call each climb and descent, and why, while you fly
Ask for the altimeter reading at each quarter of the turn
Have the learner fly it alone first and grade the altitude swings
steps.why: When the learner tells while you do, you can tell a misconception from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The line, not the altimeter, shows pivotal altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

steps.s: Heading upwind in the first turn, the learner holds altitude and presses inside rudder; the ball moves outside.
options: Let it run so the learner sees the result
Coach: center the ball with rudder and ease down to put the line back on the pylon
Tell the learner to steepen past 40° to tighten the turn
Take the controls at once and end the lesson
steps.why: Upwind the pivotal altitude is lower, so descend [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]; rudder is for coordination only [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]. Rudder-yawing at low altitude and steep bank should not be attempted, so do not let it run [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

steps.s: Rolling out toward the second pylon, the learner points straight at it with no crab and drifts north.
options: Accept it, since drift does not matter between pylons
Steepen the next turn to make up for it
Climb to the downwind pivotal altitude early
Coach a wind correction angle to the south, aiming downwind of the second pylon at the first distance
steps.why: Roll out with the proper wind correction angle so you arrive downwind of the second pylon at the same distance as from the first [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

steps.s: Twenty-five minutes in, the learner tires and the altitude swings grow.
options: Keep going until the eights are perfect
Switch to steep turns to keep things moving
Stop the maneuver, debrief it, and schedule more training
Have the learner fly lower to make the pylon easier to see
steps.why: When a learner cannot reach the proficiency level in the allotted time, the instructor should be prepared to schedule additional training [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
